sermon.title: Fitting the Mark
sermon.speaker: Pastor David G. Kincer
sermon.summary: In “Fitting the Mark,” Pastor David G. Kincer asks how anyone can meet the Bible’s requirement of righteousness, and answers with Abraham: a man full of fear and failures who was counted righteous because he believed God could do what he promised. He then applies this to seeing past our failures, to the church, and to taking the word of God to people.
sermon.transcript_source: This transcript comes from YouTube’s automatic English captions, which supply the timing and the words. Punctuation, capitalization and paragraphing were added by hand, and obvious caption errors were corrected; his wording was not rewritten. “[unclear]” marks a word or name that was not clear. Editor note: he gives the references “Romans 14:18” (the passage he reads is Romans 4:18) and “Genesis 18:30” (the promise to Sarah is in Genesis 18:10-14). The recording ends abruptly as he begins the story of two blind men from Matthew 9:27. The captions garble a place name he repeats (“Elenor”) and a few other words, shown as [unclear]. His remarks about mission trips and third-world missionaries are his own views.

chunks.section_question: How can a human fit the “mark of righteousness” when no one is righteous? (Genesis 12:2-3)
chunks.short_answer: He says the Bible “requires righteousness to inherit his promises,” yet “there’s none righteous, no, not one.” To find out how, he looks at Abraham, who was promised “a great nation,” a great name and protection, and that through his seed “all the families of the earth” would be blessed.
chunks.text:
From creation to the book of Revelation, the Bible requires righteousness to inherit his promises, his benefits of life eternal, health, the necessity of necessities of life, the fruit of the Spirit like joy, peace, longsuffering and so forth, and all the rest. Remember when they came out of Egypt, God promised the blessings in the city, the blessings in the field, the blessings on the offspring, your children’s children. They said none would be barren among you. “I will bless you with food, I’ll bless you with houses, and I’ll bless you by having none of these diseases of Egypt to come upon you, if you obey my word and do right,” fitting into that mark of righteousness. But how can a human fit into that righteous goal and that righteous requirement when the Bible says there’s none righteous, no, not one, and all of sin to come short of the glory of God?

To find out how we can, let’s take a look at a man that obtained the goal, and that is Abraham. God came to Abraham in Genesis 12:2 and said, “I’m going to make you a great nation. I am going to bless you. I’m going to make your name great. I’m going to make you a blessing to other people. I’ll bless those that bless you and curse those who curse you.” I’m going to protect you from those that hate you and despise you and want to misuse you. “I’m going to protect you, and you shall all the families of the earth be blessed.” In other words, Jesus Christ is going to come through your seed, and Jesus did, he fulfilled that by coming and turning people from sin to righteousness. In Genesis 13:16 he said, “I will make your seed as the dust of the earth.”

chunks.section_question: What did God promise Abraham and Sarah, and how impossible did it sound? (Genesis 13:16; 18)
chunks.short_answer: He says God promised Abraham a seed “as the dust of the earth,” and that Sarah, “barren” and ninety, would have a son: “I’m going to change her, renew her, restore her.” He says it also included “tribulation four hundred years,” which “we don’t like to hear.”
chunks.text: I’m going to multiply you unbelievably many times. Genesis 18:30: “Sarah your wife will have a son,” though she’s barren, though she’s past it, she’s ninety years old and she can’t have kids anymore and she’s hobbling around and she’s wrinkled and gray. “I’m going to change her, renew her, restore her, and she’s going to have a son in her old age, and you at a hundred years old and her at ninety.” And he says your seed’s going to have tribulation four hundred years. We don’t like to hear that part of “you’re going to have some troubles.”

chunks.section_question: What failures did Abraham have, and was he still counted righteous?
chunks.short_answer: He lists Abraham’s failures: lying about Sarah “out of fear for his own life,” running from the land during famine, and having a child by Sarah’s maid, which led to “a broken home.” He says Abraham even “laughed at God,” “and yet Abraham received every one of these promises because he believed God, and it was counted to him for righteousness.”
chunks.text:
Now this, you got to remember, sound impossible to Abraham. Here God’s talking to one man, an old man who’s married to an old woman who has wanted a child for decades and not got one. Abraham sees himself as old, ready to be put on the shelf, ready for retirement. His wife is old besides. He sees his failures in some areas to do right. He had lied twice about Sarah being his sister, not his wife, out of fear for his own life. He put Sarah on the line twice. He ran from the land that God told him to live in because of famine, because of economic hardships. He ran. Abraham had a lot of fear. He had a child by Sarah’s maid, which caused a rift in the family, till it wound up Ishmael, the son born to the maid Hagar, mocked and bullied Isaac, who was born later, so that Hagar and Ishmael left the family to make it on their own.

So he had a child that ran away from home. He had a broken home. You think you’re the only one that has broken homes today? Jesus Christ himself was raised with a stepdad, and then no stepdad at all, just the dad died. The provider of the home was dead. Abraham laughed at God when God said Sarah would have a child at ninety years old. He laughed. Yeah. Sure. Yeah, I hear Christians all the time laughing, “Oh yeah, sure, yeah, sure,” at things of God. See, these were impossibilities to Abraham to [unclear] on his own, and yet Abraham received every one of these promises because he believed God, and it was counted to him for righteousness. In spite of his failures, in spite of his mistakes, in spite of laughing at God when God said, “I’m going to do the impossible with you,” yet Abraham fit into this mark.

He obtained righteousness. It was counted unto him the righteousness because he what? Believed God.

chunks.text: Now, isn’t that powerful? Now, what kind of faith did Abraham have? You know, today we have the prosperity faith, we have the positive thinking faith, we have the possibility thinking faith, we have the purpose-driven faith, all these P’s. You got your [unclear] faith, you got the grunt and grit and say, “I got faith.” We, we, we really look at our own faith. “Oh, do you believe? I got the faith, I got the faith, I’m a man of faith, I’m a woman of faith.” But Abraham, what kind of faith did he have? Okay, Romans 14:18, talking about Abraham, who “contrary to hope”... chunks.section_question: What does “contrary to hope” mean, and what did being “fully convinced” look like? (Romans 4:19-21)
chunks.short_answer: He says “contrary to hope” means “expectation,” and that Abraham “expected God to fulfill what he said he would do.” He says his faith was not his own power but “Abraham’s faith in God’s faithfulness,” “being fully convinced that God … was able to perform.”
chunks.text:
“Contrary to hope” means expectation. “Contrary to hope, in hope Abraham believed, so that he became the father of many nations.” He expected God to fulfill what he said he would do. “Not being weak in faith, he did not consider his own body already dead at a hundred years old and the deadness of Sarah’s womb.” Not being weak in what? Faith. What kind of faith did this guy have? “He did not waver at the promise of God through unbelief, but was strengthened in faith, giving glory, giving honor to God.” How many would you like to be strengthened in faith? Yeah. Did Abraham need strengthened in faith? Yeah. He laughed at God. His faith was really lacking. He mocked God. Romans 4:21: “Being fully convinced that God had” what? “God had promised, God was able to perform.”

That was his faith that was put onto his account as righteousness: that God had the power to perform what he promised. Not Abraham had the power. It wasn’t Abraham’s faith, it was Abraham’s faith in God’s faithfulness, and it was what counted into him to righteousness. And we can today fit into that mark by believing like Abraham believed.

chunks.section_question: Could Abraham receive God’s promises with a broken family and few believers around?
chunks.short_answer: He says Abraham’s father was dead, his household was broken, and only three believers were in Canaan: “things don’t have to be perfect for you for God to bless your life.” He says that despite his failures Abraham “repented” and believed that God “had the power to do what God said he would do.”
chunks.text:
Now remember, Abraham’s father was dead. You know, your dad might have ran off somewhere, died, or your mom early, you know, things can happen in life. It did not stop Abraham from obtaining the promises, because of the faith that he had in God to perform. Things don’t have to be perfect for you for God to bless your life. Now that’s a good amen. He and his family, which were three people, him, Sarah and Lot, were the only believers in Canaan land. They were the only ones that worshiped God and did not worship idols. They were the only ones that believed to live right, stay married, marry one woman, stay married and so forth. Now, Abraham messed up with the maid, but he didn’t do that again. When they had church, there was only three there.

Everybody else laughed at him, mocked at him. See, things weren’t great for Abraham here. Then Lot, his nephew, got mad, and they had a quarrel and Lot left. Now there’s two. And as I said before, he conceived a child out of God’s will, he was afraid for his life and left the land to live in a pagan land, twice put Sarah’s life on the line, and Sarah did it. She went into Pharaoh’s household and went along with the program, laughed at and questioned God. And yet, in spite of this, Abraham repented of his failures and saw past the impossibilities of the promises, because he believed God had the power to do what God said he would do. That was his faith. His faith was not in his faith. Sarah’s faith was not in Abraham’s faith or her faith.

chunks.section_question: What did Abraham begin to see above his failures? (Hebrews 11:10)
chunks.short_answer: He says Abraham “began to see above himself, above his failures,” saw a city “whose builder and maker was God,” and knew that “if God said it, then it’s going to happen.” He says the faith that makes you righteous is faith “in God to perform what he promised.”
chunks.text:
Their faith was in God to perform what he promised, and that’s the faith that makes you righteous.

Now, church, that’s good stuff. Abraham, you remember in the Bible, saw a city without foundations, or a city with foundations, made without human hands, whose builder and maker was God. He began to see above himself, above his failures, and he began to see what God was talking about. He saw a great nation, he saw a great name, he saw that he was going to be blessed by God. He knew it was going to come. If God said it, then it’s going to happen. He saw that Sarah could have a child in her old age though she was barren. Remember, the Bible says Christ is our treasure in earthly vessels. You say, we, and the Bible says, “Christ be formed in you.” Folks, we can have Christ formed in us. This is our treasure in earthly human vessels, that Christ can be formed in, birthed in us, be born again of the Spirit of God.

chunks.section_question: How can Christ be formed in us, and can we see a “glorious church”? (2 Corinthians 4:7; Galatians 4:19)
chunks.short_answer: He says our faith “should be in my God, that he has the power to back up what he said,” not in being “good enough.” He asks whether we see a “failed church with a bunch of sin,” or see “past” that to a “glorious church” that God is building.
chunks.text:
These things look impossible, but if God said he can do it, then our faith should be in the fact that, not in my “good enough,” not in my righteousness, not in my faith, but my faith should be in my God, that he has the power to back up what he said, and by God, he’ll do it in my life, and that makes us righteous and fits in to the mark. Can we see today past our failures and impossibilities and see a glorious church without spot or wrinkle or any such thing that Jesus is coming for? Or all we see is a failed church with a bunch of sin going on? Or do we see past and see how God sees, that he is out to make and build a glorious church? Abraham saw the great nation, the great name, the blessing, the protection and this child being born.

He saw past his failures, and I submit to you, by the kind of faith Abraham had, we can see past our failures and others’ failures and get our eyes focused on what God told us to get focused on, and then we’ll begin to obtain them. Could that be an amen?

Can we see that God has people in California, in spite of the way California is going? God wants to complete his work in you. Amen, and form Christ in you and actually get your position of righteousness up to a condition of righteousness, where you live rightly and talk rightly. Could that be an amen? See, can we see that? Can we see, [unclear], that God can reach many in [unclear], in California, and America, the nation? Yes. chunks.short_answer: He says on the mission field “we paint houses for them” though “they’re very capable of painting and repairing,” and “very capable of preaching.” He says “what we got to take to the nations of the world is the word of God,” and that “Paul didn’t go and paint buildings. He went and preached the word.”
chunks.text:
Folks, they’re very capable of painting and repairing, and to be honest with you, they’re very capable of preaching. But what we got to take to the nations of the world is the word of God.

When you start painting, you think that’s a mission field? You go over there and you do something that they can do. Paul didn’t go and paint buildings. He went and preached the word, isn’t that right? I mean, you’re reading the same Bible I am. And I saw people over there shouldn’t have been over there. One guy met in the airport that I knew was abusing his wife, he was a tyrant in the home, and he told me I was coming back and he was leaving, and he told me he was going to the mission field. I thought, my God, you are a mission [unclear]. You know, we get hyped up on this. “I’m going to a third world country.” You better get your own act together. Could that be an amen? And we need to take this word.

chunks.section_question: What does he say the nations need, and what is the “finished work”? (Matthew 9:27)
chunks.short_answer: He says “the third world nations is sick and tired of these kind of missionaries” who take donated items, and “what they need is the word of God.” He says God promised to complete his work, and that believing God has power to do it “is my righteousness.” The recording ends as he begins a Bible story of two blind men following Jesus.
chunks.text:
If we can’t get the word in our own life and live it in our own life and teach it, our, what good are we going to do the third world nations? And honestly, the third world nations is sick and tired of these kind of missionaries. Oh, they’ll take your money, and they’ll take your chairs that you donate, your Bibles you donate, and they’ll sell them. But what they need is the word of God. Adults, are you out there? I’m telling you some facts. God promised to complete his good work. Okay, God, you said you’re going to do the job, I’m believing you have power to do it. That is my righteousness, and that’s what’s going to lead me to what? The finished work. Matthew 9:27: let’s give some stories in the Bible where this faith worked.

scriptures.text_nkjv: When Jesus departed from there, two blind men followed Him, crying out and saying, “Son of David, have mercy on us!”

faqs.question: What does he say the Bible requires to inherit God’s promises?
faqs.answer: He says “from creation to the book of Revelation, the Bible requires righteousness to inherit his promises,” including life eternal and health.

scriptures.text_nkjv: I will make you a great nation; I will bless you And make your name great; And you shall be a blessing. I will bless those who bless you, And I will curse him who curses you; And in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed.”

faqs.question: What did God promise Abraham?
faqs.answer: He says God promised to “make you a great nation,” “bless you,” make Abraham’s name great, and “protect you from those that hate you,” so that through his seed “Jesus Christ is going to come.”

scriptures.text_nkjv: I will make you a great nation; I will bless you And make your name great; And you shall be a blessing. I will bless those who bless you, And I will curse him who curses you; And in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed.”

faqs.question: How old does he say Sarah was when God promised her a son?
faqs.answer: He says she was “ninety years old,” “barren,” “hobbling around and she’s wrinkled and gray,” and Abraham was “a hundred years old.”

scriptures.text_nkjv: And He said, “I will certainly return to you according to the time of life, and behold, Sarah your wife shall have a son.” (Sarah was listening in the tent door which was behind him.) Now Abraham and Sarah were old, well advanced in age; and Sarah had passed the age of childbearing. Therefore Sarah laughed within herself, saying, “After I have grown old, shall I have pleasure, my lord being old also?” And the LORD said to Abraham, “Why did Sarah laugh, saying, ‘Shall I surely bear a child, since I am old?’ Is anything too hard for the LORD? At the appointed time I will return to you, according to the time of life, and Sarah shall have a son.”

faqs.question: What mistakes does he say Abraham made?
faqs.answer: He says Abraham “had lied twice about Sarah being his sister,” “ran from the land that God told him to live in because of famine,” and “had a child by Sarah’s maid.”

scriptures.text_nkjv: Now there was a famine in the land, and Abram went down to Egypt to dwell there, for the famine was severe in the land. And it came to pass, when he was close to entering Egypt, that he said to Sarai his wife, “Indeed I know that you are a woman of beautiful countenance. Therefore it will happen, when the Egyptians see you, that they will say, ‘This is his wife’; and they will kill me, but they will let you live. Please say you are my sister, that it may be well with me for your sake, and that I may live because of you.”

faqs.question: Does he say Abraham laughed at God?
faqs.answer: Yes. He says “Abraham laughed at God when God said Sarah would have a child at ninety years old,” yet “it was counted to him for righteousness.”

scriptures.text_nkjv: And he believed in the LORD, and He accounted it to him for righteousness.

faqs.question: What kinds of faith does he say we have today?
faqs.answer: He lists “the prosperity faith,” “the positive thinking faith,” “the possibility thinking faith,” and “the purpose-driven faith, all these P’s.”

scriptures.text_nkjv: who, contrary to hope, in hope believed, so that he became the father of many nations, according to what was spoken, “So shall your descendants be.”

faqs.question: What does he say “contrary to hope” means?
faqs.answer: He says “contrary to hope means expectation,” and “in hope Abraham believed, so that he became the father of many nations.”

scriptures.text_nkjv: And not being weak in faith, he did not consider his own body, already dead (since he was about a hundred years old), and the deadness of Sarah’s womb. He did not waver at the promise of God through unbelief, but was strengthened in faith, giving glory to God, and being fully convinced that what He had promised He was also able to perform.

faqs.question: Whose faith does he say was counted as righteousness?
faqs.answer: He says “it wasn’t Abraham’s faith, it was Abraham’s faith in God’s faithfulness,” that “God had the power to perform what he promised.”

scriptures.text_nkjv: and being fully convinced that what He had promised He was also able to perform.

faqs.question: Does he say things must be perfect for God to bless you?
faqs.answer: No. He says “things don’t have to be perfect for you for God to bless your life,” and that Abraham’s father “was dead” and it “did not stop Abraham from obtaining the promises.”

scriptures.text_nkjv: I will make you a great nation; I will bless you And make your name great; And you shall be a blessing. I will bless those who bless you, And I will curse him who curses you; And in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed.”

faqs.question: How many believers does he say were with Abraham in Canaan?
faqs.answer: He says it was “three people,” “him, Sarah and Lot,” the “only ones that worshiped God and did not worship idols,” and “when they had church, there was only three there.”

faqs.question: What does he mean that “his faith was not in his faith”?
faqs.answer: He says “their faith was in God to perform what he promised, and that’s the faith that makes you righteous,” not faith in themselves.

scriptures.text_nkjv: for he waited for the city which has foundations, whose builder and maker is God.

faqs.question: What does he ask about seeing a “glorious church”?
faqs.answer: He asks, “Can we see today past our failures and impossibilities and see a glorious church without spot or wrinkle” and not only “a failed church with a bunch of sin going on?”

scriptures.text_nkjv: that He might present her to Himself a glorious church, not having spot or wrinkle or any such thing, but that she should be holy and without blemish.

faqs.question: What does God say to Paul in Acts 18:10 as he tells it?
faqs.answer: He says God told Paul, “I am with you,” and “No man shall hurt you, for I have much people in this city.”

scriptures.text_nkjv: for I am with you, and no one will attack you to hurt you; for I have many people in this city.”

faqs.question: What does he say about people who go on the mission field?
faqs.answer: He says “Paul didn’t go and paint buildings. He went and preached the word,” and that people going abroad should “get your own act together” first.

faqs.question: What does he say third-world nations need?
faqs.answer: He says they are “sick and tired of these kind of missionaries” who bring items that get sold, and “what they need is the word of God.”
